title: Wrongs Against a Neighbor and the Fire That Never Goes Out
summary: Verses 1-7 finish the guilt offering: someone who has cheated a neighbor over a deposit, a theft, extortion, or lost property and then lied under oath must repay in full, add a fifth, and bring a ram. From verse 8 the LORD speaks to Aaron and his sons about their duties. The altar fire must never go out, the priests eat the grain offering in the holy place, the high priest's own grain offering is burned whole, and the sin offering is eaten by the priests unless its blood was taken inside the tent.
story: The first section of Leviticus, written from the side of the ordinary worshiper, ends here with sins against other people. The chapter insists that cheating a neighbor is also unfaithfulness against the LORD (verse 2), so the two cannot be pulled apart; the offender cannot settle things with God while leaving his neighbor unpaid. Then, at verse 8, the audience changes. The instructions now go to Aaron and his sons, and the offerings of chapters 1 to 5 are covered again from the priests' side of the altar, a section that runs to the end of chapter 7. These are the working rules for men who will handle holy things every day. They prepare for chapters 8 to 10, where Aaron and his sons are ordained and begin their service, and where two of Aaron's sons will die for offering fire the LORD had not commanded.
historical:
In a world without banks, people left valuables, animals, and goods with neighbors for safekeeping, and disputes followed. Exodus 22:7-13 deals with such deposits, and where no evidence existed the case was settled by an oath before the LORD (Exodus 22:11). The Laws of Hammurabi, from Babylon in the eighteenth century BC, also contain a series of laws on goods left in safekeeping, requiring witnesses and a written agreement. Leviticus 6 addresses the person who got away with it: he kept what was entrusted to him, stole, extorted, or pocketed something he found, and then swore falsely that he had not. No court has caught him. The law speaks to his conscience and gives him a way back if he comes forward, repays, and adds a fifth. Numbers 5:6-8 adds a detail for the case where the wronged person has died and left no relative: the payment then goes to the priest.

The rest of the chapter reflects the daily running of a sanctuary. Temples across the ancient world kept altar fires, received offerings, and fed their priests from them. Israel's regulations are unusually concerned with keeping the holy and the common apart, a concern still visible centuries later in Ezekiel's vision of a restored temple, where priests must change out of their linen garments before going to the people “so that they do not transmit holiness to the people with their garments” (Ezekiel 44:19).
cultural:
Priests wore linen when serving at the altar (verse 10), as Egyptian priests were also known to do. Linen was cool and plant-based, and Ezekiel 44:17-18 later forbids wool because it makes the wearer sweat. Even the humble chore of removing ashes was done in the sacred garments, but the priest changed clothes before carrying the ashes outside the camp. Every morning he added wood, laid out the burnt offering, and burned the fat of the peace offerings, and the fire was never allowed to die out.

The chapter also assumes that holiness behaves almost like a physical force. Anything that touches the most holy offerings becomes holy (verses 18 and 27). A garment spattered with sin offering blood must be washed in the holy place. A clay pot used to boil sin offering meat must be broken, since porous clay absorbs what is cooked in it, while a bronze pot can be scoured and rinsed. Most holy offerings, such as the grain offering, sin offering, and guilt offering, were eaten only by male priests in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. The priests' share of the peace offerings was less restricted and could be eaten by their families in any clean place (10:14).
literary: English and Hebrew Bibles number this chapter differently. Verses 1-7 in English Bibles are 5:20-26 in Hebrew Bibles, and English 6:8 is Hebrew 6:1, so the priestly section begins its own chapter in Hebrew. From verse 8 the material is organized by a repeated heading, “this is the law of”, followed by the name of an offering: the burnt offering (verse 9), the grain offering (14), the sin offering (25), and in the next chapter the guilt offering (7:1) and the peace offering (7:11). Inserted among these is the high priest's own daily grain offering (verses 19-23). The paragraph on the burnt offering hammers one point three times: the fire must be kept burning (verses 9, 12, and 13). The order also differs from chapters 1 to 5. The most holy offerings, reserved to the altar and the priests, come first, and the peace offering, the one of lesser holiness that lay worshipers could eat, moves to the end.

outline.t: The guilt offering for wronging a neighbor
The burnt offering: the fire must never go out
The grain offering: the priests' holy portion
The high priest's daily grain offering
The sin offering: most holy food for the priests

doctrines.note: Sin against a neighbor is sin against God (verse 2), and it cannot be put right with God while the neighbor is left unpaid. Repayment comes first, on the day the offender admits his guilt, and only then the offering at the altar.

The case of verses 1-7 is someone no court has caught. The law invites him to come forward, confess, and make the victim whole with a fifth added. Repentance here is voluntary, costly, and aimed at repairing the harm done.

Holiness is treated as real and powerful. What touches the most holy offerings becomes holy, and holy and common things must be kept apart. The priests are the guardians of that boundary for the whole community.

words.note: Torah, instruction, here translated law. It comes from a verb meaning to teach or direct. In this chapter and the next it is a technical term for the ritual procedure of each offering, the law of the burnt offering and so on. Later the same word names the whole of the first five books and, more broadly, God's teaching for his people.

Piqqadon, deposit, something entrusted to another for safekeeping. The related verb means to appoint, visit, or take charge. Keeping a deposit was a test of trust between neighbors, and betraying it is here counted as unfaithfulness toward God.

Tamid, continually or regularly. It describes the fire that must never go out (verse 13) and elsewhere the daily morning and evening offerings. Later Jewish tradition used the word as the name of the regular daily sacrifice itself.

christ: Jesus taught the same order as verses 1-7: “First go and be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:24). When Zacchaeus the tax collector met Jesus, he promised to repay anyone he had cheated fourfold (Luke 19:8), going beyond the fifth required here to the fourfold penalty the law set for stolen sheep (Exodus 22:1), and Jesus answered, “Today salvation has come to this house” (Luke 19:9). The fire that must never go out has sometimes been allegorized, but the New Testament's closest parallel is thematic: Hebrews describes a priest whose service never stops, since “He always lives to intercede for them” (Hebrews 7:25). And the chapter's contagious holiness finds a surprising echo in the Gospels. Under the law, the unclean usually defiled the clean. When Jesus touched lepers and the dead, cleanness and life flowed the other way.

hard.q: What does it mean that anything touching these offerings becomes holy?
hard.a:
Verses 18 and 27 echo earlier statements about the altar and the tabernacle furnishings (Exodus 29:37; 30:29). In ancient Israel holiness was not only a moral quality but a status, the condition of belonging to God, and the text treats it as transferable by contact. An object that touched the most holy offerings came under God's claim and could not simply return to common use, which explains why a spattered garment is washed in the holy place and a clay pot is broken.

Interpreters differ on the details. Some understand the Hebrew as a statement of fact, that contact transfers holiness. Others read it as a warning, that whoever touches must be holy, so that only consecrated priests may handle these foods. Many think the rule applied mainly to objects rather than people. The prophet Haggai later asked the priests of his day whether holy meat could make other food holy through the fold of a garment, and they answered no, while agreeing that contact with a corpse did pass on defilement (Haggai 2:12-13). The point beneath all these readings is that holiness in Leviticus is not a feeling; it is a real claim of God that changes how things may be used.

questions: The man in verses 1-7 has never been caught. What does it take to come forward and repair a wrong that no one else knows about?
Why might God insist that repayment to a neighbor come before an offering at the altar? Is there someone you need to make things right with before worship feels honest?
The altar fire needed fresh wood every morning. What daily habits keep devotion from burning out in an ordinary life?
